hints: Focus on what the two different tests are really testing, the identity of the negative ion in this white salt.
Recall the colour and ammonia solubility trend: $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute ammonia, $\text{AgBr}$ dissolves in concentrated ammonia, but $\text{AgI}$ stays solid.
Think about reducing power down Group 17 with concentrated sulfuric acid, only the strongest reducing halide can reduce sulfur all the way to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
walkthrough:
**Use the silver nitrate test to find the halide**

Silver ions give a precipitate with halides, but their behaviour in ammonia is different. This is the classic identification test.

$$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{X}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$

**Apply the ammonia solubility rule**

$\text{AgCl}$ is white and dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3$. $\text{AgBr}$ is cream and dissolves in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$. $\text{AgI}$ is yellow and does not dissolve even in concentrated $\text{NH}_3$.

Since the precipitate does not dissolve when ammonia is added, it must be silver iodide. So G contains $\text{I}^{-}$.

**Check with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is an oxidising acid. How far it is reduced depends on the reducing strength of the halide: $\text{Cl}^{-}$ gives only $\text{HCl}$, $\text{Br}^{-}$ gives $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$, but $\text{I}^{-}$ is the strongest reducing agent and reduces it all the way to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.

$$8\text{H}^{+} + 8\text{I}^{-} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 4\text{I}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{S} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify G**

Both tests point to iodide. Of the options given, only sodium iodide, $\text{NaI}$, is a white iodide salt. It fits both observations perfectly.

options.A: Caesium chloride contains $\text{Cl}^{-}$. It would give white $\text{AgCl}$ which dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, not an insoluble precipitate. With concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ it gives only $\text{HCl}$ gas, no reduction to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
options.B: Lithium bromide contains $\text{Br}^{-}$. It would give cream $\text{AgBr}$ which dissolves in concentrated ammonia, so it would not stay insoluble. With concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ it gives $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{SO}_2$, but bromide is not strong enough to produce $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
options.C: Potassium sulfate contains $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, not a halide. It gives no silver halide precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_3$ under these conditions, and warming with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ does not produce $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
options.D: Sodium iodide contains $\text{I}^{-}$. It gives yellow $\text{AgI}$ which is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia, matching test 1. Iodide is a powerful reducing agent and reduces warm concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ plus $\text{I}_2$ vapour, matching test 2.
